title: ESDC Wellness Gym: SharePoint Redesign

star.situation: The Workplace Mental Health team's resource hub lived on ESDC's legacy intranet, where they couldn't update content without IT and employees struggled to find anything.
star.task: Move it to SharePoint so the team maintains it directly and 40,000 employees can find resources without getting lost.
star.action: I ran four moderated interviews to understand how employees reach for mental-health resources, built personas, then tested the proposed information architecture with two rounds of tree testing (29 participants). Three resources scored below 30%. I pulled the career page out of the wellness IA, surfaced the CIRC crisis resource into a homepage Quick Links rail, and relabeled the Diversity Network.
star.result: The revised architecture shipped as a working SharePoint site the team owns and updates without IT tickets, with an FAQ for employees new to SharePoint.

star.situation: A federal mental-health team had access to AI tools but no clear, safe way to adopt them.

star.action: I tested agentic AI and RAG systems, designed personalized AI workflows for the team, and aligned the approach with the psychological factors behind healthy workplace adoption. title: City of Calgary: Digital Equity Pilot

star.situation: Calgary funded a pilot to test 7 essential digital services with residents most affected by the digital divide: newcomers, older adults, and people with disabilities who use assistive tech. People with disabilities were hardest to recruit, since our criteria required them to test independently on a desktop.
star.task: Recruit and run usability testing across four groups of eight, on timeline and budget.
star.action: I built a referral program with monetary incentives, sent personalized outreach for snowball recruitment, and added pre-interviews to walk candidates through what to expect. Those calls surfaced that several screen-reader users preferred their phones, so I documented it and pushed to relax the desktop-only criterion.
star.result: We mapped 18 equity challenges across all 7 services, the City proposed a follow-up round adding mobile testing, and one tester became an advocate who referred others. The results are still discussed across the City's digital teams.

star.situation: Calgary Economic Development's WIL program built a website and employer portal to connect students with placements, with part of the portal run by a third-party vendor.
star.task: Evaluate usability and inclusiveness across two phases and recommend prioritized fixes.
star.action: I ran moderated remote usability tests with scripts adapted per user group, plus heuristic analysis and accessibility testing with a screen-reader user. After two projects where vendor constraints surfaced late, I rebuilt the client-intake process to ask up front about third-party tools and limitations.
star.result: Delivered usability and heuristic reports across both phases on time, prioritized fixes with an impact-effort matrix tied to client constraints, and improved intake so future projects scoped vendor limits correctly.

star.situation: IncluCity ran inclusive research for municipal, nonprofit, and social-impact clients, with researchers of varying experience and no shared operating system.
star.task: Build the operations layer that lets a volunteer-heavy research org deliver consistent, high-quality work at scale.
star.action: I built a research-operations framework for 50+ researchers covering onboarding, training, contract administration, data management, and QA. I supported proposals and client acquisition from first contact through delivery, and ran inclusive-design workshops and panels.
star.result: The framework standardized how projects ran across the org, I delivered 140+ stakeholder interviews into client-ready reports, and inclusive-design events reached 100+ attendees.

star.situation: Beneva, one of Canada's largest mutual insurers, wanted to know where its online quote flow lost users.
star.task: As part of a four-person team, evaluate the home and auto quote experiences and rank what to fix first.
star.action: We ran moderated usability tests with surveys, scored the experience with SUS, and rated each finding by severity. The clearest failure showed up when participants edited a home quote: the price card still read $0.00 because the Recalculate Price button sat above where people had stopped looking. Six of twelve missed it and concluded the system was broken.
star.result: We delivered a SUS baseline of 79, eight prioritized fixes with severity ratings and an impact-by-effort matrix, and recommended dynamic pricing as the lead change so price updates without a button.

title: Tech3Lab: GenAI Tutoring Study (Thesis + FLAIRS)
methods: Multimodal physiological measurement (eye-tracking, pupillometry, EEG, ECG)

star.situation: AI tutors personalize learning. We had little direct evidence of how that personalization affects a learner's cognitive load in real time.
star.task: Design and run a study measuring how Generative AI personalization changes behaviour and cognitive load, rigorous enough for both a thesis and a publication.
star.action: I designed the full study from literature review and ethics through data collection, then captured multimodal physiological signals (eye-tracking, pupillometry, ECG, EEG) while participants worked through AI-mediated tasks. I analyzed the combined behavioural and physiological data to read cognitive load instead of relying on self-report.
star.result: The work became my master's thesis (honours with great distinction, 3.85 GPA) and a conference-track FLAIRS publication, with design recommendations for AI tutor systems. I was lead author on the related paper on LLM-based personalized math tutoring.

title: UQAM SEXODEV: Workflow Automation
job: UQAM SEXODEV (Workflow Automation & Process Optimization Consultant)
methods: AI workflow design (recordings to tasks / summaries / docs)

star.situation: A research chair's small remote team was buried in manual coordination. Notes were scattered across OneDrive and SharePoint, follow-ups depended on whoever took notes, and the Chair carried too much operational load.
star.task: Diagnose the bottlenecks and build a system that cuts that load and improves accountability.
star.action: I started with stakeholder interviews to find where work actually stalled, then designed AI-driven workflows that turn meeting recordings into assigned tasks, individual action summaries, and filed documentation. title: Notion to AI to Anki Pipeline

star.situation: My Johns Hopkins coursework lived in Notion as text, tables, and lecture screenshots. Reading it back didn't make it stick, and hand-writing Anki cards was slow enough that I never kept up.
star.task: Point a tool at a Notion page and get reviewed spaced-repetition cards out the other end, while staying in control of what I study.
star.action: I wrote the architecture as a spec first, then directed Claude Code to build a two-stage pipeline. Stage one reads the full page and screenshots and sends them to a vision model that returns atomic question-and-answer cards, which land in a review file I prune. Stage two loads the approved cards into Anki through AnkiConnect.
star.result: The first run produced 58 accurate cards from 1,876 content blocks and 137 screenshots for about two cents, and the model derived 25 hierarchical week tags on its own from my lecture headings. None needed deleting. The manual step that kept me off spaced repetition is gone, and the review checkpoint stayed in by design.

star.situation: Complete Complaints Foundation was validating a new website across five user segments (career seekers, members, founders, investors, partners) and wanted to know how each group read the initial design before beta. We had no tester pool of our own and depended on the client's contact list, which meant rebooking sessions several times as the client's timeline slipped.
star.task: Run moderated usability testing that surfaced barriers per segment (language, accessibility, navigation) and hand back prioritized, usable findings on a compressed schedule.
star.action: I ran project operations and moderated eight virtual sessions using a dynamic script that swapped in segment-specific questions, so a founder and a career seeker were each tested against the tasks that mattered to them. I paired the sessions with an accessibility pass and a quantitative survey, then reported lean in Miro to keep the client oriented without a long document.
star.result: Testing showed the site carried too much text and scrolling, that the search bar needed to be more prominent, and that terms like "Insights" and the partner-versus-sponsor distinction confused people. The client left with concrete design fixes: cut copy, surface search, and differentiate buttons from tags.

title: BRDGE: Usability Evaluation

star.situation: BRDGE, a food-ordering startup, wanted usability testing that would also teach their team to run research themselves. The engagement drifted from the statement of work I had proposed. The client kept changing the script and the site mid-project and stayed heavily involved in moderating sessions, which added load onto a small, low-budget team already short on leads.
star.task: Deliver credible findings on the ordering experience while managing a client who wanted hands-on control of the research.
star.action: I stepped into the lead role and brought on more volunteers, delegating the work so a small team could still ship. We ran seven moderated sessions with a heuristic and accessibility pass, then reported findings as a simplified user journey the client could act on without wading through a long deck.
star.result: The findings held up. Participants who hit bad design also reported lower trust in the service, and confusion over portion sizes, prices, and product photos left people unsure about their orders, which pointed at the information hierarchy as the core problem. The lesson I carried forward is that client-moderated sessions bias results regardless of the client's UX training, and it changed how I scoped client involvement in later projects.

title: University of Calgary Active Living: Usability Evaluation

star.situation: The University of Calgary's Active Living site and registration portal carried three heavy processes: equipment rentals, program signups, and class registration. The client wanted to know how a diverse set of users moved through them and where navigation, language, or accessibility got in the way.
star.task: Test all three flows across diverse user groups and staff a large project through volunteer turnover.
star.action: I split coverage across two scripts that each started at a different entry point and reached more of the site together than one session could, then ran twelve remote facilitated sessions with six testers per group, including a screen reader user. On the operations side, the project's size strained team lead retention, so I managed staffing and handoffs to keep sessions moving.
star.result: Testers struggled to find membership information, their cart, and course availability, and hit confusion in the booking and rental steps. The screen reader user met unlabeled links and sections that were hard to move through. The finding that traveled furthest was that pricing and program details only appeared after account login, which gave people a reason to abandon signup before they had enough to decide.

star.situation: Platform Calgary ran usability testing across two phases, and by phase two we were bringing back participants from phase one to see how the experience had changed. The client wanted to pack more into each session than an hour allowed.
star.task: Hold the line on session quality while keeping a delayed project from eating into the resources other IncluCity projects needed.
star.action: I pushed back on lengthening the sessions and explained the reasoning: past about an hour, participant attention drops and answer quality falls with it, so stretching the script only trades data quality for a couple more tasks. We kept sessions tight, ran twelve participants in phase one and eight in phase two with two returning, and I managed the schedule so the client's delays did not pull staff off other work.
star.result: The client got cleaner data from focused sessions and a phase-over-phase read on the same participants, and IncluCity's other projects kept their people and timelines.

star.situation: On a YWCA evaluation, I staffed a team lead I rated highly, and early on she started causing delays. The deliverable had shifted from what we scoped, outside pressures were mounting, and she reached a point where she did not feel she could commit to the role.
star.task: Keep the project moving and treat the team lead fairly while doing it.
star.action: I moved her off the lead role, brought in more team members to cover the gap, and went back to the client to ask for more time rather than ship late or thin. Afterward I sat down with her to hear how it had gone from her side, and I owned that I had not brought her perspective into the plan as early as I should have.
star.result: We delivered a PURE and heuristic evaluation on the revised timeline. The bigger return was operational. I started bringing leads into timeline and scope conversations from the start and set expectations with clients earlier. I also got more honest with myself about how to estimate timelines. Asking for more time is fine when you flag it early.

star.task: Contribute to a usability evaluation while getting up to speed on IncluCity's people and process.
star.action: I worked project operations on an eight-participant moderated usability study, from recruitment and scheduling through to the final presentation, and used it to understand how a volunteer-heavy research team coordinates real client work.

star.situation: Shift was recruiting for a long-term study, the kind that asks participants to stay engaged and check in every few months. The population was specific and vulnerable, so a poor match would drop out partway and cost the study time it could not spare.
star.task: Recruit, screen, and onboard participants who would stay the course, working as a team of one.
star.action: I owned recruitment from end to end. I pre-screened against tight criteria, then walked each candidate through what a multi-month commitment with recurring check-ins actually asked of them, so people signed on knowing what they were agreeing to. Retention over that timeline came down to fit, so I treated screening as the part of the work most worth getting right.
star.result: I delivered eleven screened, prepared participants matched to the study's population and set up to stay engaged through its check-in cycle.

star.situation: Rainforest was the largest study IncluCity had run to that point, around twenty participants, which was more than double our usual recruitment effort. That scale made both the logistics and the volume of data harder to manage cleanly.
star.task: Recruit and run a study at a size the team had not handled before, and keep the data organized enough to report on.
star.action: I led recruitment for the twenty participants and set up Coda for the first time to manage participants and testing data as the study grew. Getting the data structure right up front was what kept a study this size from turning into a pile we could not sort later.
star.result: We ran and reported the study, and the recruitment and data-management setup I built here carried into how I ran recruitment and data on later projects. This work is also how I first connected with Rainforest, which later brought me on directly as a project management contractor (see the Rainforest Alberta coordinator card).
